boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's engagement at Campo Tenese (9 March 1806) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1806 group: Reynier's attack on the fortified Neapolitan position on the plateau of Campo Tenese, held by Damas's troops (his corps, the left of two, in Koch; the left of his army corps in Damas), and their rout and retreat toward the Crati. The fights at the Guaro (Gauro) and Lagonegro before it, the pursuit after 10 March and the evacuation of Calabria are context. Side A is the French. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 6,000 men under General of Division Reynier and side B (Neapolitan) 10,000 men under Lieutenant-General Count Damas. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Neither other account gives the strength of either side at Campo Tenese on 9 March. Koch gives Reynier's corps 12,632 men with 12 guns at the reorganisation of the army, of whom 6,000 were already concentrated near Nocera before the march (claim koch-side-a), and Damas's corps 15 battalions and 6 squadrons, about 12,000 (claim koch-side-b); Damas gives his army corps twelve thousand, four thousand of them raw recruits (claim damas-side-b). Bodart's 6,000 is Koch's number for the men concentrated near Nocera; the passages read do not show that he took it from there. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the French (6,000 men) under General of Division Reynier over the Neapolitans (10,000 men) under Lieutenant-General Count Damas'.

claims.value: Side A (French), its own account in Koch: at the reorganisation of the army the 2e corps, destined for the conquest of the Calabrias, had 12,632 men of all arms with 12 guns, 6 of them mountain guns, under General Reynier; 6,000 of its men were already concentrated near Nocera, the rest quartered around Naples. Reynier's corps of four brigades, one of advance guard and one of reserve, marched from Salerno at the beginning of March in three columns a day apart; its advance guard was the 1er and 23e légers under General Compère. On the 9th Reynier closed the last two columns up on the first; at Campo Tenese a battalion of the 42e was sent onto the heights on the left to support the voltigeurs of the 1er léger, the advance guard formed opposite the redoubts with Verdier's division in second line, and General Franceschi's brigade of chasseurs à cheval, held back in the defile of San Martino, could not take part. Koch gives no total for the force engaged.
claims.rationale: Side A's history, read from the page images. The 12,632 is the corps' strength at the reorganisation before the march, not the force engaged on 9 March; Koch dates the reorganisation only in the OCR, so the date is not restated. The corps was the one the army's organisation gave Reynier, so the claim is tagged inherited; his dispositions on the day are in claim side-a-command. claims.value: Side B (Neapolitan), its commander's own account in Damas: he asks whether he should have disputed the ground with a French army with quite an inadequate force, and, introducing his sketch of the Calabrian provinces, asks the reader to suppose his army corps composed of only twelve thousand men, four thousand of them raw recruits; by his own note the troops that left Naples were 5000 men, mere half-clothed conscripts, and 7000 coming from the Abruzzi through Puglia were to meet him in Calabria. The corps was divided into good and very bad troops (OCR); he placed a small flying column of his best troops between the wings (OCR) and meant to put his recruits in the Campo Tenese redoubts. At Campo Tenese his left met the attack with untried and weary troops, two battalions of seasoned troops among them, recruits in the curtains and redoubts and troops on the hill on the right. He gives no total for the force at Campo Tenese.
claims.rationale: Side B's commander's account, read from the page images except the two classes of troops and the flying column (OCR); interested and self-justifying. The 5000 and the 7000 make the twelve thousand (our arithmetic). The editor's note to the twelve thousand says it probably does not include the corps of Marshal Rosenheim, which General Duhesme estimated at 7000 men; Koch has Rosenheim command a separate right corps (claim koch-side-b), while Damas presents himself as commanding an army corps with a right and a left wing and does not name Rosenheim in the passages read (claim side-b-command). The force was what he was given, so the claim is tagged inherited; his deployment is in claim side-b-command.

claims.value: Reynier commanded side A and directed the attack. In Koch, Reynier received the order to penetrate into Calabria, and a council presided by Joseph, with Masséna present, agreed that Reynier would attack the left corps while Duhesme engaged the right. Learning that the main body of the royal army awaited him in an entrenched camp at Campo Tenese, Reynier set out on the 9th at daybreak, closed up his columns, drove off a hundred or so Neapolitan horse on reconnaissance, entered the defile of San Martino with flankers on the mountains, and as his column debouched detached several companies of voltigeurs onto the mountains right and left of the plain; the attack had to be pressed despite snow and fog; learning that the heights had been swept and the enemy's right outflanked, he ordered General Compère to beat the charge and advance with the bayonet and Verdier's division to support him. In Damas, three divisions under General Reynier pursued him; Damas's editor notes that only Reynier and Verdier were major-generals and that Compère, a brigadier, commanded the advanced guard.
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions as Koch gives them, read from the page images; Damas's account and his editor's note name the commanders but not their decisions. The council set the attack on Damas's corps (claim posture); the conduct of the attack on the 9th was Reynier's, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Koch, '[the expeditions] begun by Duhesme, and Reynier received the order to penetrate into Calabria'; 'in accordance with what was decided in a council presided by Joseph, at which Massena was present, it was agreed that Reynier would attack the left corps while Duhesme engaged the right one'; 'General Reynier, learning that the main body of the royal army awaited him in an entrenched camp at Campo Tenese, a high plain surrounded by mountains, which has two narrow valleys for entrance and exit, set out on the 9th at daybreak, closed up the last two columns on the first, and after a short halt at Rotonda drove off a hundred or so Neapolitan horse that had come to reconnoitre'; 'he then entered the defile of San Martino, having the mountains that border it explored by flankers'; 'the enemy outposts were driven back by our scouts, and as soon as the head of the column began to debouch he detached several companies of voltigeurs onto the mountains to the right and left of the plain of Campo Tenese'; 'yet the attack had to be pressed', as in claim koch-side-a; 'Reynier, learning that the heights have just been swept, that two battalions, charged with their defence, are in flight, and that the enemy's right is thus outflanked, orders General Compère to beat the charge and advance with the bayonet, and Verdier's division to support his movement'.

claims.value: Damas commanded side B at Campo Tenese. By his own account he commanded the Neapolitan army corps, with headquarters at Castrovillari behind its two wings (OCR), the prince settled at Cosenza (OCR), and the generals of the two wings under orders to attack the enemy as soon as he advanced with the same intention (OCR). He had made redoubts on the Campo Tenese, meaning to place his recruits there and hold the position for a day or two while the two wings joined on the Coscile or the Crati. Reynier surprised the left wing at its post (partly OCR); its general, Marshal Minutolo Canosa, betrayed by his spies and without proper precautions, lost his head, abandoned the finest natural position in the world, and was followed to Lauria and driven back from it. Damas hurried to join him; the right wing had to retire without delay, and he determined to use the fortified position of Campo Tenese to check the enemy with his left and join the two wings; there Canosa, drunk, led one of the two seasoned battalions into imprudence; when the recruits and the troops on the right-hand hill fled, Damas gave the order to retire and returned with those who could obey to the appointed position on the Crati. In Koch, Damas commanded the left corps and had chosen his position in soldierly fashion, judging the heights almost inaccessible; the crown prince and his brother had stayed at Cosenza.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as Damas gives them (page images except the headquarters, the prince's residence, the orders to the wing generals and the start of the sentence on the surprise, OCR), with Koch's view (page images). The accounts differ on the command: Koch has two corps, the right under Marshal Rosenheim and the left under Damas, under the crown prince (claim koch-side-b); Damas commands an army corps of two wings, names Minutolo Canosa as the general of the left wing, leaves the general of the right unnamed in the passages read, and has that general break a bridge behind Cassano in his own retreat (OCR). Damas's editor identifies Minutolo Canosa as Marshal Raimondo Capece-Minutolo, one of the Princes of Canosa. Damas chose and fortified the position and ordered the retreat, so the claim is tagged commander_created; by his own note the prince's wish to hold the pass nearest Naples set the forward line (claim side-b-objectives). English renderings (ours): Koch, as in claims koch-side-b and fortification, and 'the crown prince and his brother, who out of prudence had stayed at Cosenza'.

claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side A (French) under Reynier over side B (Neapolitan) under Damas on 9 March. Koch: the defenders of the redoubts, seeing the French crown the heights, answered the first volleys with a few ill-aimed cannon shots, abandoned the redoubts and fled to the first line; no manoeuvre was attempted, the two lines mixed before they were reached, and the exit of the plain was choked with baggage and fugitives; the voltigeurs came down from the heights and cut the road to Morano; Damas could rally only 2,000 men and 200 horses, whom the bad roads and the severe season let him take away unmolested; those who escaped reached the mountains under cover of fog and night; the crown prince and his brother left Cosenza for Reggio; Marshal Rosenheim, learning of the defeat, fell back behind the Cocile (OCR); Reynier pushed on to Castro Villari on the 10th. Damas: his recruits and the troops on the right-hand hill fled, the enemy turned the rest, the fog kept him from controlling the retreat, several battalions fell into the enemy's hands, and he returned to the Crati with those who obeyed his orders; in the course of thirty hours he lost by desertion five battalions of infantry and a regiment of cavalry with their officers; he had the field-guns that could not go beyond Cosenza spiked there (OCR); four thousand men passed the lighthouse to Sicily and as many came from Cotrone, and he left the kingdom on 19 March 1806.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending (page images except Rosenheim's retreat and the guns spiked at Cosenza, OCR). Both accounts have the Neapolitan position carried and its defenders routed; the evacuation of Calabria concerns the campaign, not the engagement. The edition's introduction says the day was lost at the outset by the disorder and flight of Damas's men (OCR); Damas's editor adds that the defeat was followed by a regular dispersion of the troops, and quotes Napoleon to Joseph, 31 March 1806, that Damas could do nothing effectual with such bad troops. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and '1806 9/3. engagement at Campo Tenese (5.)'; Koch, 'the redoubts are soon reached; their defenders, seeing the French crown the heights that General Damas had judged of almost inaccessible approach, answer the first musketry volleys with a few ill-aimed cannon shots, abandon the redoubts and flee onto the first line'; 'no manoeuvre to defend the ground is attempted; the disorder is such that the two lines mix before being reached; soon the exit of the plain is choked by the baggage and the crowd of fugitives'; 'meanwhile our voltigeurs come down from the heights and cut the road to Morano'; 'Count Damas could rally only 2,000 men and 200 horses, whom the difficulty of the roads and the excessive severity of the season allowed him to take away without being troubled by the victors'; 'those who could save themselves reached the mountains, favoured by the fog and the night, which covered them with their shadows'; 'the crown prince and his brother ... no longer thinking themselves safe there, made for Reggio, escorted by a battalion of the guard and a regiment of cavalry'; 'had hastily withdrawn behind the Cocile' (p. 176, OCR); 'Reynier, not wishing to leave General Damas time to establish himself in the gorges that might have favoured the junction of the remains of his corps with the right one, still intact, moved from Morano on the morning of the 10th on Castro Villari'.

claims.value: Bodart describes Campo Tenese as a mountain plateau in southern Italy, province of Basilicata, south of the town of Lauria. Koch: a high plain surrounded by mountains, with two narrow valleys for entrance and exit, reached by the French through the defile of San Martino; the Neapolitan wings rested on heights; the exit of the plain led to Morano; at the moment of attack snow fell in large flakes and the fog grew so thick that nothing could be seen five or six paces ahead. claims.rationale: Ground and weather from Bodart's location and the two accounts, read from the page images; no map was inspected. Damas chose the position, but the ground and the weather are tagged inherited. open_questions: Deferred: P. L. Courier's letter on the action, Marulli and Duthilt's Mémoires, which Damas's editor cites, and Duhesme's estimate of Rosenheim's corps, none inspected; French reports of the action, which the passages read do not cite; Koch's account of the fights of 6 to 8 March before the action (OCR, read and not cited); Damas's narrative of the retreat after the Crati to Monteleone (OCR, cited only for the guns spiked at Cosenza); Koch's pièce justificative n° III (see the next item). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: Damas's date of setting out from Naples, the prince's distance behind his headquarters, the number of men the prince pledged to raise, the guns spiked at Cosenza and the horse the commander of the right wing brought; Koch's prisoners and guns of the fights of 6 to 8 March and the date of the army's reorganisation; the page numbers of the OCR quotes.

Most consequential gap: the strengths engaged on 9 March. Bodart gives 6,000 French and 10,000 Neapolitans; Koch gives Reynier's whole corps 12,632 at the reorganisation, 6,000 of them already concentrated near Nocera, and Damas's corps about 12,000, with no figure for the forces at Campo Tenese; Damas gives his army corps twelve thousand and no figure for the force there. The targeted follow-up read Koch's pièce justificative n° III in the parent OCR (pp. 401-403, the composition of the army of Naples at its reorganisation): it lists Reynier's corps by regiment, but its figures are garbled in the OCR and it is a state before the march, not of 9 March, so it was not registered and does not close the gap. Damas's losses by desertion after the action and the editor's prisoner figures do not give his strength on the field.

Disputes recorded in the claims: the Neapolitan strength (Bodart 10,000; Koch about 12,000 for Damas's corps and about 18,000 for both corps, whose parts make about 20,000; Damas twelve thousand for his army corps, which his editor thinks excludes Rosenheim's); the Neapolitan command (Koch: two corps under Rosenheim and Damas; Damas: one army corps of two wings under his command, the left under Minutolo Canosa); the Neapolitan loss (Bodart 3,000 mostly prisoners with 2 generals and 100 officers and all guns; Koch 1,900 prisoners with two brigadier generals, 100 officers and a guard battalion, and the artillery; Damas's editor about 2000 prisoners, more than 100 officers, and Marulli's 250; Damas has field-guns spiked at Cosenza after the retreat, without saying whether they had been at Campo Tenese); the location (Bodart: Basilicata, south of Lauria; Damas's editor: the outskirts of Calabria between the border and Morano).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 2 generals and 100 officers agree with Koch, and his 6,000 and 3,000 are not in the passages read as such); Koch (the French history of 1850 from Masséna's papers and the war depot; second-hand for Neapolitan figures); Damas (side B's commander's memoir, written by the account of the manuscripts in Sicily before his departure for Vienna, in a 1913 English translation; interested and self-justifying), whose editor's notes cite Duhesme, Courier, Marulli and Duthilt and are not independent of them. No passage read shows dependence between Koch and Damas's narrative.
